title: Module 4 · Lesson 2 — Scaling agents on Kubernetes

lines: Welcome to lesson two: scaling agents on Kubernetes.
Agent systems scale as two separate tiers, and confusing them is the classic mistake.
At ten a.m., tickets for a stadium tour go on sale.
The venue's help agent gets forty thousand questions in the first minute.
The autoscaler watches CPU, and CPU sits at twenty percent.
Meanwhile the GPUs are saturated, requests queue, and fans wait a minute for a reply.
The first tier is agent orchestration: CPU-bound, mostly waiting on I/O, and cheap to copy.
Keep it stateless, and scale it on request rate and concurrency.

say.0: The first tier is agent orchestration: CPU-bound, mostly waiting on I O, and cheap to copy.

lines: The second tier is model inference: GPU-bound, expensive, and usually the real bottleneck.
Scale it on queue depth, batch occupancy, or a latency target, typically with KEDA.

say.1: Scale it on queue depth, batch occupancy, or a latency target, typically with keda.

lines: Even on the right signal, a new GPU replica can take minutes to start.
It must pull a huge image, load weights into GPU memory, and load the engine.
So pre-cache the model with the NIM Operator's NIMCache, so pods skip the download.
And keep a warm floor of replicas, because scale-to-zero is wrong for latency-sensitive services.

say.0: So pre-cache the model with the nim Operator's nim cache, so pods skip the download.

lines: Trigger scale-up at sixty to seventy percent capacity, not ninety-five.
Then the new replica is ready before the rush, not after it.
Sometimes one GPU must serve several workloads.
MIG slices it in hardware, with dedicated compute and memory, for hard multi-tenant guarantees.

say.1: Mig slices it in hardware, with dedicated compute and memory, for hard multi-tenant guarantees.

lines: Time-slicing has no isolation, so keep it for dev and test.
MPS offers partial isolation, and latency-critical inference gets a dedicated GPU.

say.1: M P S offers partial isolation, and latency-critical inference gets a dedicated GPU.

lines: After the sale comes the bill, and the biggest saving is routing by difficulty.
A small classifier sends easy questions to a small model, and hard ones to a large one.
Next, cache repeated answers and the shared system prompt.
Then shrink the agent loop, distill a small model from production traces, and batch what can wait.
Measure cost per successfully completed task, not cost per token.
A cheaper model that fails and needs extra steps can cost more per resolved question.
On the exam, never autoscale GPU inference on CPU utilization.
Scale on queue depth or latency with a warm floor, then read on for the details.
